content: This document is an updated version of a Cochrane review originally published in 2011. It focuses on vulval intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN), a pre-malignant condition affecting the skin of the vulva. VIN is a rare but chronic condition that carries a significant risk of recurrence and has the potential to progress to vulval cancer. The disease is particularly challenging to manage due to its tendency to present in multiple areas (multicentric) and in multiple forms (multifocal). The incidence of VIN appears to be increasing, especially among younger women. There is no consensus on the optimal surgical treatment for VIN. The primary goals of surgical intervention are to alleviate symptoms, rule out any underlying malignancy, and preserve the anatomy and function of the vulva. However, repeated surgical treatments can negatively affect the cosmetic appearance of the vulva and lead to psychosexual issues, which in turn can significantly impact a patient’s quality of life. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of surgical interventions for women with high-grade VIN. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to September 1, 2015. Additional sources, such as clinical trial registries, conference abstracts, and reference lists of relevant studies, were also reviewed. Experts in the field were contacted for further information. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared different surgical interventions in adult women diagnosed with high-grade VIN. Data collection and analysis were performed independently by two reviewers, who also assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. Only one RCT, involving 30 women, met the inclusion criteria. This trial compared carbon dioxide (CO2) laser surgery with cavitational ultrasonic surgical aspiration (CUSA). After one year of follow-up, there were no significant differences between the two groups in terms of disease recurrence, pain, scarring, dysuria or burning, adhesions, infection, abnormal discharge, or eschar formation. However, the trial had limited statistical power due to the small sample size and the low number of observed events. Despite this limitation, the trial was deemed to have a low risk of bias. The authors concluded that the lack of statistical power in the included trial, combined with the small sample size and limited number of events, prevents any definitive conclusions from being drawn about the effectiveness and safety of CO2 laser surgery versus CUSA for the management of VIN. As a result, there is insufficient reliable evidence to provide clear guidance or recommendations for clinical practice regarding these surgical techniques.
